questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was important for me to choose a destination that was not so different from my home country that I would not be able to get comfortable there in the 5 months of exchange. I'm a bit shy, so going to a place where I for example would have to learn the language as well as adapt to a different culture WHILE studying would be overwhelming to me. So, going to the Netherlands was the perfect balance of a somewhat familiar cultural environment while still allowing me to explore a new country on my own, making international and local friends, and studying without stressing too much about the external environment.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Best experience of my life, hands down. I would recommend anyone considering studying abroad to do it!!!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, lots of nice personnel and exchange mentors available to answer questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: No assistance needed for me as we were kept very well informed about introductory activities before arriving.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I booked a room through the university's housing service, which gave me a discount voucher to spend with a private landlord offering rooms to students of EUR. Because of the housing crisis in the Netherlands, I jumped on the first opportunity to secure a room and thus took the offer from HouseHunting Rotterdam. I'm now very glad that I got it out of the way quickly and did not have to stress about it after November, but I cannot fully recommend the place in spite of the fantastic location. he owners are disorganized, rude and will try to get away with charging extra fees that are not disclosed in the rental contract. So, it is a decent place to live if you are an independent person who can stand up for yourself, write a good complaint and be persistent with the administration. If not, I would try to live on-campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I found it really rewarding to keep my "home life" separate from my university life. Living off-campus allowed me to meet people who were not students but just residents, and to widen my circle outside of student life. I'm also not a party animal, so living on-campus with the young guns would not suit me. I mostly just really liked settling into my local area, and I ended up falling in love with my little corner of the city, which I came to consider my home and feel super comfortable in.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Super easy, you get to browse the course catalogue some time before registration opens, and then you just put in the course numbers that you want, when the registration portal opens.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Lots of help! I asked a bunch of questions to the incoming exchange coordinator who was very kind to answer them all. But I did not need any help with the practical things around registration as the uni sent out many informative emails regarding deadlines and guidelines for registration and late registration as well.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very, because the School of History, Culture and Communication did not offer any classes within the fields of history or culture that semester for international master students, so I had to take three communications classes that I initially did not really care for. They turned out very interesting though.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Really research the past years' course offers before you accept an offer from the host uni! Also make sure to ask your home uni about their agreement with the host uni, so you know whether you can maybe take lower or higher-level courses if the courses on offer for you own level is too small.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level of the courses a bit too easy for me as a master student, but this is probably because a master's degree in NL is only one year, so the courses have to be short and remain somewhat introductory...

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The professors were extremely organized which I really appreciated, and easy to contact. I however wish they would encourage more engaged class discussions, as two of my professors were too lax with the students, and just allowed them to be completely quiet behind their screens in the back of the room – or sometimes allowed students to talk amongst themselves which really disturbed the learning environment.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Strategic Mass Communication
Digital Citizenship and Community Engagement
Digital News Media

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Strategic Mass Communication with professor Étienne Auge! Still a somewhat 101-style course, but definitely my favorite of the ones I took. The professor forbids electronic during class, so notes are taken on paper, and students are much more focused and engaged due to the absence of screens. The professor is also very active and WILL ask you a question if he believes you are zoning out. So, his teaching style is not for the faint of heart who want to be left alone in the back, but it will be a huge help come exam time, when you find out that you remember so much more than when you took notes on the computer.

questions.answer: None that were unexpected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Taking the trains intercity trains between the bigger cities in the Netherlands can be really expensive, so look into getting an OV-card so you can discounted trips either off-peak hours on weekdays or on weekends.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very very satisfied!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The EUR is very dedicated to promoting student well-being through social activities outside of studying, so there were lots of options! I really recommend checking out the Studium Generale organisation and signing up for events such as talks, movie screenings and art cafes. The univerisyt also arranges field trips to famous destinations in NL, such as the Koekenhof Tulip Gardens, for really good prices. Use these offers!!!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really really recommend going to the OpenHeART Cafés where students get to do arts and crafts on campus in a chill environment and no pressure to do great art, just have fun. Shout out to the ladies who put on the bead jewelry workshop. I joined the ErasmusPride club and went to some cool events with them.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Utrecht, it's so cute! Go to Amsterdam for an entire day or stay for a few if you have the time. Do not miss out on going to the beach in the Hague during the summer, it's beautiful and quite close. Explore Rotterdam Zuid which is extremely underrated.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, as I stated, it was important to me that I would be able to adjust quickly so that cultural differences would not become a stressor. Dutch people are super kind and the citizens of Rotterdam are very laid-back, so settling in was super easy, and if you learn the basic shop phrases, they'll love you for it.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Dutch food is not good, so look for foreign cuisines if you want to eat out, which you will end up doing.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I found the residents to be super open to foreign students who want to engage with the local culture. I really appreciate how much Dutch people like to have a good time and listen to live music and drink beers in the sunshine.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Do your research to make sure that you can get courses that you'll like and that fit within you programme at UCPH.
2. You'll have to work hard to find Dutch friends, as EUR is mostly internationals. Get into local cultural events, volunteer maybe.
3. Rent a bike through Swapfiets, it'll save you so much money in the long run.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not be discouraged if you don't score as high grades as you're used to. Apparently the professors are quite strict with their grades, and the point scale allow them to go into great detail with the grade.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Studying was fun and challenging sometimes, but the best part without a doubt getting to find my feet in a completely new culture on my own, building a life there how I would like it to be, and making a bunch of great friends from all over the world!!! Getting to form your own group of likeminded people and learning about their cultures was so rewarding and lovely. I'll miss my exchange pals.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The first month was a little rough. You're still settling in, classes have started and are stressful, and you haven't really made close friends with anyone yet. So everything feels kind of up in the air, but it'll get so much better with just a few more weeks. Two months in you'll have great friends and won't miss home that much anymore.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: GO ON EXCHANGE!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
